claim: Cholera toxin (CT) enters and intoxicates host cells after binding cell surface receptors using its B subunit (CTB).
source: Cholera toxin (CT) enters and intoxicates host cells after binding cell surface receptors using its B subunit (CTB).
evidence: This is a statement from the abstract that describes the mechanism of CT entry into cells, representing established knowledge in the field.

claim: The ganglioside (glycolipid) GM1 is thought to be the sole CT receptor.
source: The ganglioside (glycolipid) GM1 is thought to be the sole CT receptor
evidence: This statement reflects the prevailing view in the field prior to this study, based on established scientific consensus.

claim: The mechanism by which CTB binding to GM1 mediates internalization of CT remains enigmatic.
source: the mechanism by which CTB binding to GM1 mediates internalization of CT remains enigmatic
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field, indicating a gap in understanding.

claim: CTB binds cell surface glycoproteins.
source: Here we report that CTB binds cell surface glycoproteins.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by multiple experimental approaches including crosslinking, immunoprecipitation, and mass spectrometry.

claim: Relative contributions of gangliosides and glycoproteins to CTB binding depend on cell type.
source: Relative contributions of gangliosides and glycoproteins to CTB binding depend on cell type
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing different CTB binding patterns in Jurkat cells versus T84 and Colo205 cells (Figures 1, 2, 4).

claim: CTB binds primarily to glycoproteins in colonic epithelial cell lines.
source: CTB binds primarily to glycoproteins in colonic epithelial cell lines
evidence: This is supported by data from inhibitor studies and binding assays in T84 and Colo205 cells (Figures 2, 4).

claim: The glycan portion of CEACAM5, not the protein, provides the CTB interaction motif.
source: demonstrated that the glycan portion of the molecule, not the protein, provides the CTB interaction motif
evidence: This is supported by experiments showing that inhibition of N-linked glycosylation abolishes the CTB-CEACAM5 interaction (Figure 5D, E).

claim: Fucosylated structures promote CTB entry into a colonic epithelial cell line.
source: We further show that fucosylated structures promote CTB entry into a colonic epithelial cell line
evidence: This is supported by data showing that inhibition of fucosylation with 2F-Fuc reduces CTB internalization (Figure 9A).

claim: Fucosylated structures promote subsequent host cell intoxication by CT.
source: fucosylated structures promote CTB entry into a colonic epithelial cell line and subsequent host cell intoxication
evidence: This is supported by data showing that inhibition of fucosylation reduces cAMP accumulation in response to CT (Figure 9B).

claim: CTB-binding fucosylated glycoproteins are present in normal human intestinal epithelia.
source: CTB-binding fucosylated glycoproteins are present in normal human intestinal epithelia
evidence: This is supported by CTB-HRP blotting of normal human intestinal lysates (Figure 10B) and flow cytometry analysis of freshly isolated human colonic epithelial cells (Figure 10C, D).

claim: Vibrio cholerae is the etiological agent of cholera.
source: The bacterium Vibrio cholerae is the etiological agent of cholera (Foster and Baron, 1996).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field, supported by a citation.

claim: Cholera toxin is secreted by V. cholerae and is the direct cause of the profuse, watery diarrhea that characterizes fatal cholera.
source: Cholera toxin (CT) is secreted by V. cholerae and is the direct cause of the profuse, watery diarrhea that characterizes fatal cholera.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: CT is a heterohexamer comprising one copy of cholera toxin subunit A (CTA) and five copies of subunit B (CTB).
source: CT is a heterohexamer comprising one copy of cholera toxin subunit A (CTA) and five copies of subunit B (CTB).
evidence: This is established structural knowledge about CT.

claim: The CTB subunits of the holotoxin bind receptors on the surface of host enterocytes, enabling endocytosis of CT.
source: The CTB subunits of the holotoxin bind receptors on the surface of host enterocytes, enabling endocytosis of CT.
evidence: This is part of the established model for CT intoxication, supported by citations (Sánchez and Holmgren, 2008; Lencer, 2003).

claim: CT follows a retrograde trafficking pathway to the ER where it is disassembled to release CTA.
source: CT follows a retrograde trafficking pathway to the ER where it is disassembled to release CTA.
evidence: This is part of the established model for CT intoxication, supported by citations (Sánchez and Holmgren, 2008; Lencer, 2003).

claim: CTA enters the cytoplasm and catalyzes ADP-ribosylation of the α-subunits of heterotrimeric GTP-binding proteins (Gαs).
source: CTA enters the cytoplasm and catalyzes ADP-ribosylation of the α-subunits of heterotrimeric GTP-binding proteins (Gαs).
evidence: This is part of the established mechanism of CT action.

claim: The extended activation of Gαs leads to increased activity of adenylate cyclase, raising intracellular cAMP levels.
source: The resulting extended activation of Gαs leads to increased activity of adenylate cyclase, raising intracellular cAMP levels.
evidence: This is part of the established mechanism of CT action.

claim: Elevated cAMP causes activation of chloride channels and chloride efflux, followed by massive secretion of water and ions into the intestinal lumen.
source: Elevated cAMP causes activation of chloride channels and chloride efflux, followed by massive secretion of water and ions into the intestinal lumen.
evidence: This is part of the established mechanism of CT action.

claim: Affected individuals can experience rapid and severe dehydration, sometimes leading to death.
source: Affected individuals can experience rapid and severe dehydration, sometimes leading to death (Foster and Baron, 1996).
evidence: This is established knowledge about cholera, supported by a citation.

claim: The initial and required step in host cell intoxication is recognition of cell surface receptors by CT.
source: The initial and required step in host cell intoxication is recognition of cell surface receptors by CT.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the established mechanism of CT action.

claim: In the 1970s, the ganglioside GM1 was identified as a host cell receptor for CT.
source: In the 1970s, the ganglioside GM1 was identified as a host cell receptor for CT.
evidence: This is historical knowledge about the discovery of GM1 as a CT receptor.

claim: A lipid extract from the brain inhibited CT activity.
source: A role for gangliosides was first postulated when Van Heyningen et al. discovered that a lipid extract from the brain inhibited CT activity (van Heyningen et al., 1971)
evidence: This is a historical finding supported by a citation.

claim: Purified gangliosides inhibited CT binding, with GM1 the most potent inhibitor.
source: subsequently, multiple groups showed that purified gangliosides inhibited CT binding, with GM1 the most potent inhibitor (Cuatrecasas, 1973; Holmgren et al., 1973; King and van Heyningen, 1973)
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: Exogenous GM1 incorporated into host cell membranes increased sensitivity to toxin.
source: exogenous GM1 was incorporated into host cell membranes, where it was shown to increase sensitivity to toxin, (Cuatrecasas, 1973)
evidence: This is a historical finding supported by a citation.

claim: Exogenous GM1 sensitized toxin-resistant cells.
source: even sensitizing toxin-resistant cells (Moss et al., 1976)
evidence: This is a historical finding supported by a citation.

claim: The extent of CT binding to intestinal mucosa from several species correlated with GM1 content.
source: Holmgren and co-workers examined intestinal mucosa from several species and found that the extent of CT binding correlated with GM1 content (Holmgren et al., 1975).
evidence: This is a historical finding supported by a citation.

claim: Addition of exogenous GM1 to intestinal mucosa resulted in increased secretory activity in response to CT stimulation.
source: Further, addition of exogenous GM1 to intestinal mucosa resulted in increased secretory activity in response to CT stimulation, implying that GM1 serves as a functional receptor.
evidence: This is a historical finding that led to the inference that GM1 is a functional receptor.

claim: Recognition of GM1 occurs exclusively through the CTB subunit.
source: Recognition of GM1 occurs exclusively through the CTB subunit.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the specificity of GM1 binding.

claim: The high affinity CTB-GM1 interaction has been extensively characterized through binding assays.
source: Indeed, the high affinity CTB-GM1 interaction has been extensively characterized through binding assays (Kuziemko et al., 1996)
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: The high affinity CTB-GM1 interaction has been extensively characterized through x-ray crystallography analysis.
source: the high affinity CTB-GM1 interaction has been extensively characterized through binding assays (Kuziemko et al., 1996) and x-ray crystallography analysis (Merritt et al., 1994).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: CTB is closely related to the B subunit of E. coli heat-labile toxin (LTB) at the levels of sequence.
source: CTB is closely related to the B subunit of E. coli heat-labile toxin (LTB) at the levels of sequence, (Dallas and Falkow, 1980)
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: CTB is closely related to LTB at the level of structure.
source: CTB is closely related to the B subunit of E. coli heat-labile toxin (LTB) at the levels of sequence, (Dallas and Falkow, 1980) structure, (Sixma et al., 1991)
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: CTB is closely related to LTB at the level of function.
source: CTB is closely related to the B subunit of E. coli heat-labile toxin (LTB) at the levels of sequence, (Dallas and Falkow, 1980) structure, (Sixma et al., 1991) and function (Spangler, 1992).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: LTB is known to bind both GM1 and glycoprotein receptors.
source: While LTB is known to bind both GM1 and glycoprotein receptors
evidence: This is established knowledge about LTB binding properties.

claim: GM1 is commonly described to be the sole host cell receptor recognized by CTB.
source: GM1 is commonly  described to be the sole host cell receptor recognized by CTB (Foster and Baron, 1996).
evidence: This is a statement about the prevailing view in the field, supported by a citation.

claim: A variety of experimental approaches have pointed to the possibility that CTB may also recognize glycoproteins present on mammalian cells.
source: However, a variety of experimental approaches have pointed to the possibility that CTB may also recognize glycoproteins present on mammalian cells (Morita et al., 1980; Monferran et al., 1990; Balanzino et al., 1994; Platt et al., 1997; Hansen et al., 2005; Blank et al., 2007; Day et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a summary of previous findings supported by multiple citations.

claim: CTB binding to cells does not uniformly parallel GM1 levels, implying the existence of additional CTB-binding molecules.
source: Indeed, CTB binding to cells does not uniformly parallel GM1 levels, implying the existence of additional CTB-binding molecules (Platt et al., 1997; Yanagisawa, 2006).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from experimental observations, supported by citations.

claim: GM1 binding does not always correlate with intoxication.
source: Moreover, GM1 binding does not always correlate with intoxication.
evidence: This is a statement about observations in the field.

claim: Treatment of intestinal mucosa with V. cholerae sialidase yielded more GM1 but had no effect on toxin sensitivity.
source: For example, treatment of intestinal mucosa with V. cholerae sialidase yielded more GM1 but had no effect on toxin sensitivity (Holmgren et al., 1975).
evidence: This is a historical finding supported by a citation.

claim: A point mutant of CTB (H57A) maintained GM1 binding but the corresponding holotoxin did not intoxicate host cells.
source: Also, a point mutant of CTB (H57A) was shown to maintain GM1 binding but the corresponding holotoxin did not intoxicate host cells (Aman et al., 2001).
evidence: This is a finding from a previous study, supported by a citation.

claim: GM1 comprises only 0.01% of the glycosphingolipid content in normal human intestinal epithelia.
source: Finally, a recent analysis of a normal human intestinal epithelia found that GM1 comprises only 0.01% of the glycosphingolipid content, raising the question of whether its concentration in enterocytes is sufficient to account for intoxication by CT (Breimer et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a finding from a previous study, supported by a citation.

claim: Fucosylated molecules are recognized by CTB.
source: Here we report that fucosylated molecules and glycoproteins are recognized by CTB
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by monosaccharide competition experiments (Figure 6) and lectin blocking experiments (Figure 7).

claim: Fucosylated molecules can function as receptors in host cell intoxication.
source: fucosylated molecules and glycoproteins are recognized by CTB and can function as receptors in host cell intoxication
evidence: This is supported by data showing that inhibition of fucosylation reduces CTB internalization and cAMP accumulation (Figure 9).

claim: Glycoproteins can function as receptors in host cell intoxication.
source: fucosylated molecules and glycoproteins are recognized by CTB and can function as receptors in host cell intoxication
evidence: This is supported by data showing that inhibition of O-linked glycosylation reduces CTB internalization (Figure 9A).

claim: Glycoproteins, not gangliosides, are responsible for the majority of CTB binding to human colonic epithelial cell lines.
source: Glycoproteins, not gangliosides, are responsible for the majority of CTB binding to human colonic epithelial cell lines.
evidence: This is supported by data from inhibitor studies and binding assays (Figures 2, 4).

claim: CEACAM5 is one CTB-interacting glycoprotein.
source: Using a metabolically incorporated photocrosslinking sugar analog, we isolated and identified one CTB-interacting glycoprotein, CEACAM5.
evidence: This is supported by proteomics analysis (Table 1) and immunoprecipitation experiments (Figure 5).

claim: The carbohydrate portion of CEACAM5, not the amino acids, provides the CTB interaction motif.
source: The carbohydrate portion of the glycoprotein, not the amino acids, provides the CTB interaction motif.
evidence: This is supported by experiments showing that inhibition of N-linked glycosylation abolishes the CTB-CEACAM5 interaction (Figure 5D, E).

claim: Fucose-containing glycans are recognized by CTB, resulting in internalization.
source: We show that fucose-containing glycans are recognized by CTB, resulting in internalization, the first step in host cell intoxication.
evidence: This is supported by data showing that inhibition of fucosylation reduces CTB internalization (Figure 9A).

claim: Fucosylated glycoconjugates recognized by CTB are present in normal human tissue.
source: Finally, we report evidence suggesting that fucosylated glycoconjugates recognized by CTB are present in normal human tissue.
evidence: This is supported by CTB-HRP blotting of normal human intestinal lysates (Figure 10B) and flow cytometry analysis of freshly isolated human colonic epithelial cells (Figure 10C, D).

claim: CTB recognizes molecules other than GM1.
source: In addition, the demonstration that CTB recognizes molecules other than GM1 has important implications for the interpretation of experiments where CTB is used to study the organization of lipids in the plasma membrane.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the findings of the study.

claim: Ac4ManNDAz can be metabolized to a photocrosslinking sialic acid analog (SiaDAz) and incorporated into glycoconjugates in place of natural sialic acids.
source: Previously, we reported a cell-permeable precursor sugar (Ac4ManNDAz) that can be metabolized to a photocrosslinking sialic acid analog (SiaDAz) and incorporated into glycoconjugates – both glycoproteins and glycolipids – in place of natural sialic acids (Figure 1A) (Tanaka and Kohler, 2008).
evidence: This is a description of a previously published method, supported by a citation.

claim: Culturing Jurkat cells with Ac4ManNDAz results in production of SiaDAz-modified gangliosides, including SiaDAz-modified GM1.
source: Culturing Jurkat cells, a human T cell line, with Ac4ManNDAz results in production of SiaDAz-modified gangliosides, including SiaDAz-modified GM1 (Bond et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a description of a previously published finding, supported by a citation.

claim: CTB crosslinks to GM1 in Jurkat cells.
source: After adding CTB to these SiaDAz-producing cells and applying UV radiation, we observed crosslinking of CTB to GM1, consistent with the idea that GM1 is the CT receptor (Bond et al., 2010, 2011).
evidence: This is a description of a previously published finding, supported by citations, and confirmed in this study (Figure 1B).

claim: A CTB-containing species with apparent mass of ~13 kDa matches the molecular weight of a CTB-GM1 complex in Jurkat cells.
source: By anti-CTB immunoblot analysis of Jurkat cell lysates, we confirmed detection of a CTB-containing species whose apparent mass (∼13 kDa) matches the molecular weight of a CTB-GM1 complex (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a finding from the current study, supported by immunoblot data (Figure 1B).

claim: The CTB-GM1 complex was absent in lysates from T84 and Colo205 colonic epithelial cell lines.
source: In contrast, the CTB-GM1 complex was absent in lysates from both colonic epithelial cell lines (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a finding from the current study, supported by immunoblot data (Figure 1B).

claim: High molecular weight CTB-reactive bands were observed in lysates from Jurkat, T84, and Colo205 cells.
source: By reanalyzing the crosslinked lysates using a lower percent gel, we discovered additional CTB-reactive bands at much higher molecular weights in lysates from all three cell lines (Jurkat, T84 and Colo205; Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a finding from the current study, supported by immunoblot data (Figure 1C).

claim: Appearance of the high molecular weight CTB-reactive bands was dependent on both inclusion of Ac4ManNDAz and UV irradiation.
source: Appearance of the high molecular weight bands was dependent on both inclusion of Ac4ManNDAz and UV irradiation, suggesting that these bands also represent CTB crosslinked to sialylated molecules, but of much larger molecular weight than GM1.
evidence: This is a finding from the current study, supported by immunoblot data (Figure 1C).

claim: The high molecular weight CTB-reactive bands represent CTB crosslinked to sialylated molecules of much larger molecular weight than GM1.
source: Appearance of the high molecular weight bands was dependent on both inclusion of Ac4ManNDAz and UV irradiation, suggesting that these bands also represent CTB crosslinked to sialylated molecules, but of much larger molecular weight than GM1.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental observations (Figure 1C).

claim: CTB crosslinking patterns are cell type dependent.
source: Thus, CTB crosslinking patterns are cell type dependent, and CTB crosslinking to GM1 is not observed in all cell types.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comparison of crosslinking patterns in different cell lines (Figure 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).

claim: CTB crosslinking to GM1 is not observed in all cell types.
source: Thus, CTB crosslinking patterns are cell type dependent, and CTB crosslinking to GM1 is not observed in all cell types.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comparison of crosslinking patterns in different cell lines (Figure 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).

claim: NB-DGJ reduced GM1 production in Jurkat cells.
source: The ganglioside biosynthesis inhibitor NB-DGJ reduced GM1 production in Jurkat cells (Figure 3B)
evidence: This is a finding from the current study, supported by thin-layer chromatography data (Figure 3B).

claim: NB-DGJ resulted in a decrease in CTB binding to Jurkat cells.
source: The ganglioside biosynthesis inhibitor NB-DGJ reduced GM1 production in Jurkat cells (Figure 3B) and also resulted in a decrease in CTB binding (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is a finding from the current study, supported by flow cytometry data (Figure 4A).

claim: Culturing Jurkat cells with benzyl-α-GalNAc had no significant effect on CTB binding.
source: In contrast, culturing Jurkat cells with benzyl-α-GalNAc or kifunensine had no significant effect on CTB binding (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is a finding from the current study, supported by flow cytometry data (Figure 4A).

claim: Culturing Jurkat cells with kifunensine had no significant effect on CTB binding.
source: In contrast, culturing Jurkat cells with benzyl-α-GalNAc or kifunensine had no significant effect on CTB binding (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is a finding from the current study, supported by flow cytometry data (Figure 4A).

claim: Jurkat cells have an O-linked glycosylation defect caused by a frame-shift mutation in the gene encoding chaperone C1GALT1C1.
source: The inability of benzyl-α-GalNAc to affect CTB binding to Jurkat cells is consistent with the known O-linked glycosylation defect in these cells, caused by a frame-shift mutation in the gene encoding chaperone C1GALT1C1 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A) (Ju and Cummings, 2002).
evidence: This is established knowledge about Jurkat cells, supported by a citation and confirmed by sequencing in this study (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).

claim: Gangliosides are the dominant binding partners for CTB on Jurkat cells.
source: Thus, the inhibition studies indicate that gangliosides are the dominant binding partners for CTB on Jurkat cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the inhibitor studies (Figure 4A).

claim: NB-DGJ had no effect on CTB binding to T84 cells.
source: NB-DGJ, the inhibitor of ganglioside biosynthesis, had no effect on CTB binding.
evidence: This is a finding from the current study, supported by ELISA and fluorescence microscopy data (Figure 4B, C).

claim: Kifunensine resulted in only small effects on CTB binding to T84 cells.
source: Kifunensine, an inhibitor of N-linked glycan maturation, resulted in only small effects on CTB binding.
evidence: This is a finding from the current study, supported by ELISA and fluorescence microscopy data (Figure 4B, C).

claim: Culturing T84 cells with benzyl-α-GalNAc resulted in reductions in CTB binding.
source: In contrast, culturing cells with benzyl-α-GalNAc, which blocks elaboration of O-linked  glycans, resulted in reductions in CTB binding in both assays.
evidence: This is a finding from the current study, supported by ELISA and fluorescence microscopy data (Figure 4B, C).

claim: Glycoproteins are the dominant CTB binding partners in T84 cells.
source: We conclude the glycoproteins are the dominant CTB binding partners in T84 cells and that gangliosides do not make a large contribution to CTB binding to T84 cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the inhibitor studies (Figure 4B, C).

claim: Gangliosides do not make a large contribution to CTB binding to T84 cells.
source: We conclude the glycoproteins are the dominant CTB binding partners in T84 cells and that gangliosides do not make a large contribution to CTB binding to T84 cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the inhibitor studies (Figure 4B, C).

claim: NB-DGJ treatment did not affect CTB binding to Colo205 cells.
source: NB-DGJ treatment did not affect CTB binding to Colo205 cells (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is a finding from the current study, supported by flow cytometry data (Figure 4D).

claim: Benzyl-α-GalNAc did not cause a reduction in CTB binding to Colo205 cells.
source: However, in contrast to the results observed for T84 cells, benzyl-α-GalNAc did not cause a reduction in CTB binding to Colo205 cells (Figure 4D)
evidence: This is a finding from the current study, supported by flow cytometry data (Figure 4D).

claim: Colo205 cells lacking C1GALT1C1 did not show reduced CTB binding.
source: nor did Colo205 cells lacking C1GALT1C1 show reduced CTB binding (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is a finding from the current study, supported by flow cytometry data (Figure 4E).

claim: Colo205 cells cultured with kifunensine exhibited enhanced CTB binding.
source: Instead, Colo205 cells cultured with the N-linked inhibitor kifunensine exhibited enhanced CTB binding (Figure 4D)
evidence: This is a finding from the current study, supported by flow cytometry data (Figure 4D).

claim: Culturing Colo205 cells with kifunensine and benzyl-α-GalNAc together resulted in decreased CTB binding.
source: The only case where we observed decreased CTB binding was when the two protein glycosylation inhibitors – kifunensine and benzyl-α-GalNAc – were used together (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is a finding from the current study, supported by flow cytometry data (Figure 4D).

claim: CTB binds primarily to glycoproteins on Colo205 cells, with contributions from both N-linked and O-linked glycans.
source: Based on these data, we propose that CTB binds primarily to glycoproteins on Colo205 cells, with contributions from both N-linked and O-linked glycans.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the inhibitor studies (Figure 4D).

claim: Gangliosides do not make a large contribution to CTB binding to Colo205 cells.
source: Gangliosides do not make a large contribution to CTB binding to Colo205 cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the inhibitor studies (Figure 4D).

claim: Immunoprecipitation of CEACAM5 resulted in purification of the CTB crosslinked complex.
source: Immunoprecipitation of CEACAM5 resulted in purification of the CTB crosslinked complex (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is a finding from the current study, supported by immunoprecipitation and immunoblot data (Figure 5A).

claim: Immunoprecipitation with anti-CD44 resulted in purification of the CTB crosslinked complex.
source: Similarly, immunoprecipitation performed with anti-CD44 resulted in purification of the CTB crosslinked complex (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is a finding from the current study, supported by immunoprecipitation and immunoblot data (Figure 5B).

claim: Anti-CTB immunoprecipitated CEACAM5 efficiently.
source: We also performed immunoprecipitation with anti-CTB, which resulted in efficient purification of CEACAM5, but only weak purification of CD44 (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is a finding from the current study, supported by immunoprecipitation and immunoblot data (Figure 5C).

claim: Anti-CTB immunoprecipitated CD44 weakly.
source: We also performed immunoprecipitation with anti-CTB, which resulted in efficient purification of CEACAM5, but only weak purification of CD44 (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is a finding from the current study, supported by immunoprecipitation and immunoblot data (Figure 5C).

claim: Anti-CTB immunoprecipitated CEACAM5 even when the Ac4ManNDAz crosslinker was omitted.
source: Notably, anti-CTB immunoprecipitated CEACAM5 even when the Ac4ManNDAz crosslinker was omitted, suggesting that the CTB-CEACAM5 interaction is relatively strong (Figure 5C,D).
evidence: This is a finding from the current study, supported by immunoprecipitation and immunoblot data (Figure 5C, D).

claim: The CTB-CEACAM5 interaction is relatively strong.
source: Notably, anti-CTB immunoprecipitated CEACAM5 even when the Ac4ManNDAz crosslinker was omitted, suggesting that the CTB-CEACAM5 interaction is relatively strong (Figure 5C,D).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that anti-CTB immunoprecipitates CEACAM5 without crosslinking (Figure 5C, D).

claim: The material purified by anti-CTB and recognized by anti-CEACAM5 had a slightly higher apparent molecular weight when the crosslinker was included than when it was omitted.
source: Furthermore, the material purified by anti-CTB and recognized by anti-CEACAM5 had a slightly higher apparent molecular weight when the crosslinker was included than when it was omitted (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is a finding from the current study, supported by immunoprecipitation and immunoblot data (Figure 5C).

claim: There is direct crosslinking between CTB and CEACAM5.
source: Thus, we observe direct crosslinking between CTB and CEACAM5.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the immunoprecipitation experiments (Figure 5C).

claim: CD44 co-purifies with the CTB-glycoprotein crosslinked complex, but is not directly crosslinked to CTB.
source: Additionally, CD44 co-purifies with the CTB-glycoprotein crosslinked complex, but is not directly crosslinked to CTB.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the immunoprecipitation experiments (Figure 5B, C).

claim: Both benzyl-α-GalNAc and kifunensine treatment caused reductions in the apparent molecular weight of CEACAM5.
source: Both benzyl-α-GalNAc and kifunensine treatment caused reductions in the apparent molecular weight of CEACAM5, suggesting that this protein bears both N-linked and O-linked glycans.
evidence: This is a finding from the current study, supported by immunoblot data (Figure 5D).

claim: CEACAM5 bears both N-linked and O-linked glycans.
source: Both benzyl-α-GalNAc and kifunensine treatment caused reductions in the apparent molecular weight of CEACAM5, suggesting that this protein bears both N-linked and O-linked glycans.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that both N-linked and O-linked glycosylation inhibitors affect CEACAM5 apparent molecular weight (Figure 5D).

claim: Treatment with benzyl-α-GalNAc enhanced the CTB-CEACAM5 interaction.
source: Treatment with benzyl-α-GalNAc enhanced the CTB-CEACAM5 interaction, while treatment with kifunensine abrogated the interaction, and treatment with NB-DGJ had no effect.
evidence: This is a finding from the current study, supported by immunoprecipitation and immunoblot data (Figure 5D).

claim: Treatment with kifunensine abrogated the CTB-CEACAM5 interaction.
source: Treatment with benzyl-α-GalNAc enhanced the CTB-CEACAM5 interaction, while treatment with kifunensine abrogated the interaction, and treatment with NB-DGJ had no effect.
evidence: This is a finding from the current study, supported by immunoprecipitation and immunoblot data (Figure 5D).

claim: Treatment with NB-DGJ had no effect on the CTB-CEACAM5 interaction.
source: Treatment with benzyl-α-GalNAc enhanced the CTB-CEACAM5 interaction, while treatment with kifunensine abrogated the interaction, and treatment with NB-DGJ had no effect.
evidence: This is a finding from the current study, supported by immunoprecipitation and immunoblot data (Figure 5D).

claim: Inhibition of N-linked glycan maturation blocked crosslinking between CTB and CEACAM5.
source: Inhibition of N-linked glycan maturation also blocked crosslinking between CTB and CEACAM5 (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is a finding from the current study, supported by immunoprecipitation and immunoblot data (Figure 5E).

claim: Protein glycosylation regulates the ability of CEACAM5 to interact with CTB.
source: Thus, protein glycosylation regulates the ability of CEACAM5 to interact with CTB.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the inhibitor studies (Figure 5D, E).

claim: Additional CTB-crosslinking proteins exist in T84 cells beyond CEACAM5.
source: While culturing cells with kifunensine abolished the CEACAM5-CTB interaction (Figure 5E), overall CTB crosslinking in T84 cells was only slightly affected by kifunensine treatment (Figure 2B). Thus, additional CTB-crosslinking proteins exist in T84 cells and remain to be identified.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the comparison of the effects of kifunensine on CEACAM5-CTB interaction versus overall CTB crosslinking.

claim: Epidemiological studies implicate variation among fucose-containing glycoconjugates in human susceptibility to cholera.
source: Epidemiological studies implicate variation among fucose-containing glycoconjugates in human susceptibility to cholera (Barua and Paguio, 1977; Swerdlow et al., 1994; Harris et al., 2005; Holmner et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a summary of findings from previous epidemiological studies, supported by citations.

claim: Some glycan array binding experiments suggest that fucosylated glycans can be recognized by CTB, albeit with lower avidity than GM1.
source: In addition, some glycan array binding experiments performed by the Consortium for Functional Glycomics (CFG) suggest that fucosylated glycans can be recognized by CTB, albeit with lower avidity than GM1 (Consortium for Functional Glycomics, 2010).
evidence: This is a summary of findings from glycan array experiments, supported by a citation.

claim: Fucose is not present in GM1.
source: Importantly, fucose is not present in GM1, which is recognized by CTB through interactions with its terminal Neu5Ac and galactose residues (Merritt et al., 1994).
